newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa braces for trade union action from Monday.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa braces for trade union action from Monday.

text.p: South Africa's biggest labour federation, the 1.9 million Congress of South African Trade Unions, said on Friday it was ready to roll out a mass action campaign over controversial new proposed employment laws.
"We are going ahead nationally on Monday with a work stoppage for one hour. Everybody's geared up for the campaign," Cosatu spokeswoman Noweto Mpati told Reuters.
Cosatu affiliated unions are organised in major sectors including mining, metal and engineering, chemical and oil, motor industry and health and transport as well as the public sector.
Mpati said a good turnout was expected by the federation to back up its plans for fresh national strikes and regional action to ensure its demands over new labour legislation are enforced.

"Workers are angry that we are still in deadlock over a 40-hour week because they thought that since their political party is in government, the leadership would understand the importance of this particular demand.

"Workers are also angry that there is no clear position from the side of the government on maternity leave and how it is going to be paid...It (the mass action) is something workers are going to come out for," she said.
Cosatu is in an alliance with the ruling African National Congress (ANC) of President Nelson Mandela, stemming from the struggle against apartheid.
Since it came to power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994, Mandela's government has confounded many of its right-wing critics by pursuing market-friendly policies.

But while the government's commitment to a free market and privatisation has wooed foreign investors and South Africa's still predominantly white business community, it has provoked argument with its labour ally.
At the centre of the current controversy is the new Basic Conditions of Employment Bill which has already been approved by Cabinet and is due to be tabled in parliament by September 15.

The labour federation upped the ante with a one-day national strike on June 2 to drive home its core demands for six months' maternity leave, of which at least four should be paid, and a 40-hour working week to be phased in over five years.
Monday's stoppage will be followed by 24-hour strikes in all the major regions in the country from August 18 to August 21 -- unless agreement is reached before then.
Business objects to the two core demands, arguing that certain of the provisions in the bill could raise employment costs to the point of creating obstacles to new jobs.
Labour Minister Tito Mboweni has been hard at work attempting to broker a deal between business and labour as the September 15 parliament deadline looms.
In a bid to force them into a compromise, he has warned there is a danger of the bill "withering away" and not being legislated this year -- a fate that the unions in particular wish to avoid.
